title: Durable immune control and functional remyelination in multiple sclerosis

concept.text: The proposed innovation combines lasting control of damaging multiple sclerosis disease activity with biological repair sufficient to recover meaningful function. Remyelination means rebuilding the insulating myelin around surviving nerve fibers. Success would require that repair to improve nerve-signal conduction and help preserve those fibers, alongside control of the disease processes that could damage them again. The combined outcome remains hypothetical in the supplied record.

Conceptual synthesis: preventing new damage, repairing myelin and restoring lost neural connections are distinct therapeutic tasks. Suppressing inflammatory activity does not by itself establish that old lesions have healed or that every form of progression has stopped. Remyelination also cannot be assumed to replace severely damaged or lost axons. A selective, one-time immune reset is one possible implementation of durable disease control; it is neither an established requirement nor a demonstrated component of the combined breakthrough described here.

significance.text: Conditional significance: a safe treatment that durably prevents further damaging disease activity while repairing enough affected tissue to restore function could change MS from a continuing source of disability into a condition compatible with lasting recovery. The revolutionary consequence would be the combination of sustained protection and regained capability. Either component alone would leave a central part of the problem unresolved.

Conditional downstream possibilities include less dependence on continuing treatment and reduced need for assistance if recovery translates into sustained improvements in daily activities. Treatment-free benefit would have to be demonstrated separately from benefit maintained by ongoing therapy. Neither reduced treatment burden nor broad functional recovery follows automatically from evidence that a drug affects one measure of nerve conduction.

Conceptual limits: recovery would depend on how much repairable tissue remains and which pathways are affected. Restoring insulation around surviving axons is a different achievement from reconstructing lost axons, reconnecting circuits or recovering learned function after tissue loss. The innovation therefore does not imply universal reversal of disability, and a successful remyelination treatment would not alone justify describing MS as cured.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed capability gap: durable disease control and effective repair must be achieved together. Control must last long enough to protect repaired tissue and must be assessed against both relapses and continuing progression. A treatment intended to reset immunity would also need to preserve acceptable long-term immune function. The supplied material does not establish which intervention, or combination of interventions, could meet these requirements.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: repair must reach clinically relevant lesions, restore functional myelin around surviving axons and produce useful changes in conduction and axonal preservation. Demonstrating a response in one accessible pathway would leave open whether treatment reaches other affected regions, works in older lesions and helps patients with different disease courses. Where axons are severely damaged or absent, additional regeneration and reconnection capabilities may be necessary.

Measurement synthesis: a convincing program must connect evidence of biological repair to meaningful functional benefit. Changes in a conduction measure, structural evidence of remyelination, improvements in daily function and durable control of disease activity answer different questions. Trials must distinguish these outcomes and establish whether their benefits persist, rather than treating improvement in one measure as proof of the entire combined capability.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies the ReBUILD study by Green and colleagues, dated 10 October 2017, as a randomized, controlled, double-blind crossover trial of clemastine fumarate in relapsing MS with chronic optic neuropathy. Its account states that participants were receiving stable immunomodulatory treatment and that the trial found a change in visual evoked-potential latency consistent with a remyelinating effect. This describes a finding in visual-pathway conduction within a specific clinical setting, rather than a demonstration of the complete proposed innovation.

The interpretation is constrained by source availability. The source index lists the ReBUILD PDF as not captured, with no retained artifacts, and the supplied review had no inspectable primary-source passage with which to verify the population, design or findings. The research provides a summary and a locator to the paper’s first-page Summary and Findings, but these do not permit independent confirmation of the underlying text here. The trial account is therefore retained with that qualification; missing source capture is not evidence that the reported result is false.

On the supplied account, ReBUILD did not demonstrate repair throughout the central nervous system, an immune reset or a cure. Because the described participants were receiving stable immunomodulatory therapy, the reported latency finding also cannot establish disease control after withdrawal of treatment. No effect size, sample size or duration of benefit is supplied in inspectable evidence, so no quantitative estimate is added.

Evidence coverage limitation: the supplied bounded search record is empty, so developments through the review’s stated cutoff of 1 November 2026 cannot be assessed. The material supports retaining a qualified account of the dated 2017 result, but it does not establish the present-day state of the wider field or demonstrate that the combined breakthrough has been achieved. It also provides no basis for classifying additional results as confirmed, disputed or preprint-only.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration framework: controlled trials, followed by independent replication, should demonstrate durable control of damaging disease activity, objective evidence of remyelination, meaningful functional recovery and acceptable long-term safety. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established consensus thresholds. The trials should specify the intended patient population and disease courses so that the scope of any success is clear.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration framework

completion_criteria.text: Proposed repair and function criteria: evidence should show that relevant lesions undergo repair and that the repaired pathways provide useful function. Conduction measures can contribute, but should be interpreted alongside complementary evidence of remyelination and functional outcomes. A result confined to chronic optic neuropathy could establish benefit in that setting; broader claims would require evidence across additional affected pathways and clinical circumstances.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed repair and function criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and safety criteria: a claim of treatment-free control requires a defined withdrawal strategy and follow-up for both relapse and progression after withdrawal. A one-time cure claim would require prolonged observation, including long-term immune safety. The supplied record does not specify an adequate follow-up duration, an acceptable recurrence rate or an acceptable safety threshold; these would need explicit justification before testing.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed durability and safety criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent studies should reproduce the combined benefits with clearly described treatment protocols, outcome definitions and patient selection. Results should identify limits associated with disease course, lesion characteristics and remaining axonal integrity. Finite trials could establish the breadth of demonstrated benefit in studied populations, but could not establish literal universality or guarantee lifelong freedom from disease.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-05, “Regenerate a severely injured spinal cord with functional reconnection,” and NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” overlap with the additional repair that might be needed when MS has caused severe axonal or tissue loss. NRL-12 centers on durable disease control and functional remyelination; regenerating long connections or replacing tissue while retaining learned function introduces separate requirements. These entries remain distinct even if a future treatment combines their capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-16, “Biologically repair the injured visual pathway,” is especially relevant to the visual-pathway setting described for ReBUILD. The overlap is restoration of biological visual function. The distinction is scope: visual-pathway repair need not address MS disease activity, while an MS treatment must establish protection and benefit beyond any single pathway before supporting broader claims.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” could provide an enabling capability if effective repair requires precise delivery to relevant cells or lesions. Delivery is a separate problem from determining what intervention produces lasting immune control or functional remyelination. The supplied material does not establish programmable delivery as a necessary implementation of NRL-12.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-09, “Prevent Alzheimer’s dementia before irreversible functional loss,” and NRL-11, “Halt established Alzheimer’s disease and restore lost function,” share the distinction between preventing further injury and recovering function after injury. Their disease processes and repair requirements differ from those of MS. NRL-15, “Identify and treat shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration across diseases,” could overlap with axonal preservation, but no shared mechanism or cross-disease treatment is established by this record.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-07, “A dependable neural communication channel for profound paralysis,” NRL-08, “A visual-cortex prosthesis that restores useful, detailed sight,” and NRL-17, “A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation,” seek useful function through engineered interfaces. They could address some consequences of neurological disability, but successful communication, prosthetic vision or interface-assisted movement would not itself demonstrate immune control or biological myelin repair.

change_log.change: Preserved NRL-12’s identity as the combination of durable immune control and functional remyelination.
change_log.reason: The review found the concept coherent; limitations in supporting evidence do not justify deleting it or labeling the entire innovation unsupported.

change_log.change: Integrated the distinctions among inflammatory suppression, remyelination, axonal preservation and replacement of lost connections.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why control of disease activity and improvement in a conduction measure cannot independently establish comprehensive recovery.

change_log.change: Retained the supplied 2017 ReBUILD account while explicitly qualifying its verification and scope.
change_log.reason: The research names a specific trial, but the review and source index document no captured primary-source artifacts. That limits verification without refuting the reported result.

change_log.change: Separated the dated trial account from assessment of developments through 1 November 2026.
change_log.reason: An empty bounded search record prevents a current field assessment and does not count against an older result.

change_log.change: Kept a selective one-time immune reset as an optional implementation and made downstream benefits conditional.
change_log.reason: Neither necessity of that implementation nor treatment-free recovery is established in the supplied material.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to distinguish biological repair, functional benefit, withdrawal durability, replication and safety without inventing numerical thresholds.
change_log.reason: The review supports these as a coherent proposed framework while leaving operational thresholds unresolved.

change_log.change: Added roster-based relationships while preserving the separate identities of repair, delivery, prevention and interface concepts.
change_log.reason: Relevant overlap clarifies potential dependencies and complementary approaches without conflating their achievements.

unresolved_issues: The ReBUILD primary-source text was not captured. Its exact methods, effect size, sample size, follow-up duration and safety findings cannot be independently verified from the supplied material.
No supplied search results establish developments through 1 November 2026, so the present-day status of the combined capability remains unassessed.
The intervention or combination capable of providing both durable disease control and meaningful functional repair is unspecified.
The extent to which remyelination alone could restore function, and when additional axonal regeneration or circuit reconstruction would be required, remains unresolved for particular patient groups.
Disease-course coverage, functional endpoints, withdrawal procedures, follow-up duration and acceptable immune safety thresholds remain to be operationally defined.
